answer.why: As a public servant, 'Confirmed & Substantive' made me laugh straight away, because it is exactly the phrase you wait years to see on your letter after probation and acting appointments. Only someone who has lived the system would pick it, so I would trust the details to be right. 'Minister Salary' is the obvious hook and I have seen that joke a hundred times at kopitiam tables, so I would scroll past it as clickbait, even though I would be curious how they model the benchmarking.
answer.expect_minister_salary: A cheeky satire about the famous ministerial pay benchmark, probably a clicker or an 'earn the big paycheck' game with a bit of outsider snark. I would expect the details to be shallow and the humour to be about money, with the grades and appraisals as window dressing, and I would be braced to wince at wrong titles.
answer.expect_confirmed_substantive: A dry, insider game about the slow grind of bureaucracy: probation, acting appointments, appraisals, waiting for the promotion to be made permanent. I would expect deadpan humour about wording and process, and a more careful, authentic feel, though the name might be too obscure for outsiders to tap.

answer.held_back_by: Nothing much, really. The file put no ceiling on me, and the only real limiter was the PM seat itself, plus my own late choice to walk every block instead of running on the record, which cost STAND. Integrity kept me clean rather than held me back.
answer.ending_fair_why: I got to PM with a clean file and the declassified card tied it to a specific choice I remembered making. Retiring at 59 felt abrupt, but the card explained why.
answer.chase_next: The version where I take the party's Senior Minister of State estimate at face value and see what a compromised, ambitious path looks like, maybe with an integrity dip, to see if the PM ending is reachable another way.
answer.play_again_why: The early and middle years were interesting, but the late stretch of single-option years made it feel on rails. I'd need to know choices come back more before I'd go again straight away.

tone_breaks.note: No one becomes a Permanent Secretary at 31. It breaks the realism the rest of the game works hard to build.

tone_breaks.line: The formula pays you twice the entry-grade minister's salary, and the formula was published, so nobody can say they were not told.
tone_breaks.note: A bit of a nudge at the real salary debate. It reads as commentary, not simulation, and the PM figure is not framed that way in reality.

tone_breaks.line: Y7: attended the tea, STAND dropped
tone_breaks.note: The tea is a real insider thing and was done well, but the immediate stat drop felt too mechanical for something that is usually ambiguous.

answer.title_fit_why: The game is at its best on appraisals, nominations and quiet choices, not pay. The salary line is the hook, but what stayed with me was whether I was confirmed in my role and what I did with it.
